text: Zerops deploys what you tell it to. Notch tells you what you forgot. This is a desktop app that holds your git repository against your live Zerops account and finds the difference. Everything here runs against a real account over the real API. Nothing is mocked.

It starts with a Zerops personal access token, verified by a real call rather than by checking that it looks like a token. It is held in the daemon's memory for this session only — never written to disk, never logged, never sent anywhere but Zerops.

Let's start from nothing. Notch is explicit that this creates a real, billable project, and that it starts empty. Creating infrastructure and filling it are two different decisions, so they are two different buttons.

Now point it at a repository. This one is a Node API that needs Postgres for records, Valkey for sessions, Meilisearch for search, Qdrant for embeddings, NATS for background jobs, and object storage for uploads.

Notch reads the package manifest and the environment files and compares what it finds against what the project actually runs. Seven services missing — and they're drawn inside the project they're missing from, because a project with holes in it should look like a project with holes in it.

Every finding cites the line that produced it. Meilisearch is here because the code imports the meilisearch client. Notch never asserts a requirement it cannot point at a file for, and anything inferred only from an environment variable name is marked low confidence, because a name is weaker evidence than an import.

And this is the failure that gets through every other check. Nine variables the code reads that this project does not define. A missing service fails loudly at deploy time. A missing variable does not: the image builds, the container starts, health checks pass, and the first request that needs a signing secret throws. Notch reads the names only — never the values.

Down the side are the coding agents already installed on this machine — Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini. No API keys; Notch drives the ones you already pay for, and hands them the live state of the project, its gaps, and the evidence behind each one.

So let's ask one to draft the fix. What comes back is not a file — it's a list of services with a reason for each. The daemon builds the actual import file, resolving versions from the live catalogue. The agent gets judgement about what and why, and no authority to act.

Here's what it drafted, in the same preview a human confirms. Notice object storage was proposed and is not in the file: the catalogue has no Zerops type for it, so the agent could ask for it but could not conjure one. The secrets are Zerops generator expressions, not values — the platform generates them during the import, so nothing is copied out of your repository.
Confirm, and these are real services being created on a real account.
Six of the seven are satisfied. The seventh stays a ghost and says why, rather than being quietly dropped to make the number look better.

Now the view Zerops does not have. Zerops shows one project at a time, and one project at a time is exactly how development, staging and production drift apart. Hold two against each other and Notch compares presence, version, failover mode, public routing, and which variable names are defined.

Services are matched by type rather than hostname, because a database called db in staging and postgresql in production is the same service wearing two names. Container counts are deliberately not compared — those legitimately differ, and including them would bury the lines that matter.

But the real answer is that none of this should need a human to remember to look. The same engine runs headless. Notch check reads the repository, reads the target project, and exits non-zero when the code needs infrastructure the project has not got.

Six services and nine variables missing, each citing the dependency that proves it, as annotations on the pull request. And a check that cannot look never exits zero — if the token is wrong or the API is down it returns two and says so, because reporting all clear because you could not see would be worse than having no gate at all.

Everything is written to Postgres as it happens, so the timeline survives a reload and a daemon restart. That a service is missing right now is something anyone can compute. That it has been missing across three scans since Tuesday requires having written the earlier answers down.

That's Notch. Your repository and your infrastructure, held against each other — with the evidence for every claim, a history that remembers, agents that draft but never act, and a gate that fails the build before the merge. Zerops deploys what you tell it. Notch tells you what you forgot.
